description: Based in Quixadá, Ceará, Brazil, Sertão Vivo is led by independent developer and entrepreneur Clériston Almeida Capistrano. We aim to explore NASA data on environmental change and drought in Brazil’s semi-arid region. We welcome collaborators in Earth science, statistics, data analysis, web development and AI. Working language: Portuguese. The solution will be developed during the hackathon.
summary: Sertão Vivo helps learners investigate how rainfall and temperature have changed near Açude Cedro in Brazil’s semiarid Ceará. For Be An Earth System Trend Detective!, users select a variable and time window, explore 45 years of NASA POWER / MERRA-2 data, and inspect the rate of change and its uncertainty. Daily Funceme rainfall adds observed dry spells; NASA daily temperatures show whether selected spells were hotter than usual. The working browser prototype preserves missing observations, provides guided examples and exports data. Its value is making local evidence understandable and checkable before preparedness discussions—not forecasting drought or claiming proven mitigation.
details:
The question

How can we better understand dry periods in the sertão so that communities can discuss ways to reduce drought consequences? We start with a bounded historical question: what do rainfall and air-temperature records near Açude Cedro reveal about seasonal variability, unusual years and trends? The intended users are learners and people discussing water preparedness with local specialists. This prototype has not been tested with those users.

How it addresses the challenge

What: corrected rainfall and 2 m air temperature. Where: the NASA grid near Açude Cedro, Quixadá. How much: Sen change per decade. How certain: nominal Mann–Kendall tests plus block-resampling sensitivity intervals. Users select either variable and one of three time windows. This is a bounded single-location demonstration, with regional expansion left for future work.

Our solution

The English browser explorer contains NASA POWER monthly corrected precipitation and 2 m air temperature for 1981–2025, requested at 4.9799°S, 39.0800°W near Quixadá. Users can choose a variable, compare three documented analysis windows, inspect annual values and uncertainty, compare any year with the 1991–2020 monthly reference, and download a CSV. Two short guided investigations explain variable units and lead users from trends to a daily case. The interface also counts daily station dry spells in complete windows and compares five selected zero-rain cases with NASA daily temperatures relative to the same calendar dates in 1991–2020. It works offline, without installation, an account or a server.

What we built during the event

Using existing local-data preparation, we acquired the long NASA POWER series, audited calendar coverage and units, calculated annual and seasonal summaries, implemented trend and uncertainty analysis, built the interactive explorer, added daily dry-spell and temperature comparisons, and prepared seven English slides. The participant provided the underlying question; earlier data collection is distinguished from the analysis and prototype developed during the hackathon.

Methods

NASA POWER precipitation is a mean daily rate in mm/day, multiplied by the number of calendar days in each month. Annual temperature is weighted by days. Annual summary keys ending in 13 are excluded. Sen slopes and nominal two-sided Mann–Kendall p-values are calculated for 1981–2025, 2001–2025 and 2007–2025. The p-values assume independent years. We also report exploratory residual-block bootstrap intervals using 3- and 5-year blocks, 2,000 replicates and a fixed seed. These checks address some short-range dependence and do not establish climate attribution. No multiple-testing correction is applied across the exploratory windows.

Daily comparisons

Station sequences preserve missing readings. Within-window comparisons require every day observed: 16 complete February–May seasons are available. For temperature, we use NASA POWER daily T2M and T2M_MAX from Jan 1981 through Jul 2026, rather than deriving daily values from monthly means. Calendar-date departures use the 1991–2020 reference. Gauge intervals end at 07:00 GMT−3; NASA uses local-solar days. Matching dates is descriptive; a preceding-day match is reported as a sensitivity check.

What the results show

At this source grid in 1981–2025, the estimated rainfall slope is −12.2 mm/decade, with nominal p=0.681 and a 5-year block sensitivity interval from −77.1 to +55.9 mm/decade. The uncertain annual slope does not imply an absence of drought risk or of changes within seasons. Annual mean temperature has an estimated slope of +0.22 °C/decade, nominal p=0.010, and a 5-year block interval of +0.08 to +0.34 °C/decade. The shorter 2007–2025 temperature interval includes zero, demonstrating window sensitivity. In 2012, annual rainfall was 315.5 mm, 54.7% below the 1991–2020 reference. These are historical patterns and descriptive departures, not an official drought class or evidence of a particular cause.

During 2012, 44 zero-rain intervals from March 31 to May 13 had mean NASA temperature 2.06 °C above the same-date reference. After 8 mm on May 14, another 39 zero-rain intervals on May 15–June 22 averaged 2.30 °C above reference. Previous-day matches give 2.03 and 2.35 °C. In contrast, the 229-day zero-rain case in 1991–1992 averaged near the thermal reference (−0.16 °C departure). Selected-case duration does not identify thermal severity by itself. These are temporal associations, not causal effects.

Why local data quality matters

The archived Funceme AC. CEDRO file contains 239 of 463 possible months between Jan 1988 and Jul 2026. Only 212 months and 11 full years have complete daily coverage. Missing 999 codes and absent months are never treated as zero rainfall; partial monthly sums remain partial. COGERH Pedras Brancas records are shown separately as published storage context. Repeated published values are not assumed to be new measurements, interpolations or genuine stability. Reading rules, quality, revisions and the storage-curve version remain unresolved. Cedro rainfall is not a catchment mean for Pedras Brancas and cannot establish storage causality.

Limits and future value

This is one gridded reference location, not a regional diagnosis. The NASA monthly archive ends in 2025; the new daily archive ends in July 2026. Neither is a current alert. Daily station counts supplement the monthly analysis; their incomplete coverage does not support a historical trend. We have not estimated water demand, linked rainfall causally to reservoir storage, or demonstrated a mitigation effect. Future work should expand regional coverage, validate daily dry-spell findings and established drought indices, incorporate water use and reservoir operations, and validate the interpretation and proposed actions with local users and domain experts. The present contribution is a transparent, reproducible way to inspect evidence before making such claims.

AI assistance and originality

The participant supplied the question about understanding dry periods to help reduce drought consequences. Codex assisted with selecting sources, writing Python and browser code, exploratory calculations including the participant-requested daily dry-spell and temperature comparisons, data checks, English writing and slide preparation. Provider data were preserved; missing observations were not imputed. Charts use source data, and no generated photographs, audio or videos are included. The AI disclosure is also visible in the interface and slides. Participant review and independent scientific validation remain necessary. We do not claim autonomous scientific discovery or demonstrated mitigation effects.

Implementation tools

Python, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and HTML/CSS/JavaScript. Source snapshots, dependency versions, code and methods are available through the final-project link. All charts use the cited provider data. No NASA logos or generated photographs, audio or video are used.
